Anatomy of an HTTP call

Retrofit hides the request behind an annotation and hands you an object back. The rest of this course reads the parts it hides. Here they are, once, mapped to the Retrofit code you already write.

  • Puzzle 1: Finding the server

    Every machine on the internet has an IP address, a number that routers use to deliver packets. People and code use hostnames instead, like api.example.com. Before the first connection, the phone asks DNS, the internet's phone book, which address a hostname has. That lookup is one more round trip on a cold start, so the answer is cached for a while.

The problem

You write @GET("users/42") and get a User. When something fails, Retrofit gives you a code like 404 or 503, and later puzzles talk about parts of the request it hides. What exactly travels, and what do those numbers mean?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

An HTTP request has four parts:

PartExampleIn Retrofit
HTTP methodGET, POST, PUT, DELETE@GET, @POST…
path/users/42the annotation's string
headersAuthorization: Bearer …@Header, or an interceptor
bodyJSON of a new order@Body

The method says what you want: GET reads, POST creates something new, PUT replaces something at that path, DELETE removes it. Headers are name–value pairs about the message, not the data itself: who you are, what format you accept, how long something may be cached.

The response comes back with a status code, headers, and a body. Status codes come in families, by their first digit:

FamilyMeaningExamples
2xxit worked200 OK, 201 Created
3xxlook elsewhere, or use what you have301 Moved Permanently
4xxyour request was wrong400 Bad Request, 401, 404, 429 Too Many Requests
5xxthe server failed500, 503

The family is what your code usually decides on: a 4xx won't fix itself if you send the same request again; a 5xx might.

The analogy

A letter to an office: the method is what you're asking for ("please file this", "please send me that"), the path is which department, the headers are the notes on the envelope, the body is the letter. The reply comes with a stamp: approved, see the other office, your form is wrong, or we're closed.

Check yourself

Your app gets a 404 from GET /users/42. Should it retry the same request?

Right. 4xx won't fix itself.

Not quite. Changing the method changes the meaning; it doesn't fix a missing user.

Not quite. Only server failures (5xx) might pass; a 4xx is about your request.

Not quite. The body is the data; notes about the message go in headers.

Not quite. Status codes say how it went; caching rules travel in headers.

Sources
  • MDN: An overview of HTTP ("HTTP headers make this protocol easy to extend and experiment with"; requests and responses as HTTP messages)
  • MDN: HTTP response status codes ("Responses are grouped in five classes: Informational responses (100 – 199), Successful responses (200 – 299), Redirection messages (300 – 399), Client error responses (400 – 499), Server error responses (500 – 599)")

What you now know

An HTTP request is a method (GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, DELETE to remove), a path, headers (name: value pairs about the message) and an optional body. The response has a status code, headers and a body. Status codes come in families: 2xx worked, 3xx look elsewhere or use what you have, 4xx your request was wrong, 5xx the server failed.
